syllabus.clause: CAP as a statement about behaviour during a partition (PA vs PC)

at.step: Reveal: PA vs PC, the actual choice

syllabus.clause: PACELC adding the normal-case latency-vs-consistency trade (EL vs EC), with systems classified (Dynamo/Cassandra PA/EL, Spanner PC/EC)
failure domains (process, host, rack, AZ, region) as what "partition" means physically

sources.source: CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed (Eric Brewer)

items.item: the CAP theorem states that any networked shared-data system can have at most two of three desirable properties: consistency, availability, tolerance to partitions
allowing at least one node to update state during a partition forfeits consistency; preserving consistency means one side must act as if unavailable

at.step: Reveal: PA vs PC, the actual choice

items.item: because partitions are rare, there is little reason to forfeit consistency or availability when the system is not partitioned
in Google, the primary partition usually resides within one datacenter, with Paxos used on the wide area for global consensus

sources.source: Problems with CAP, and Yahoo's little known NoSQL system (Daniel Abadi)

items.item: PACELC: if there is a partition, trade availability against consistency; else, trade latency against consistency
Dynamo-family systems are PA/EL: they give up consistency for availability under partition, and for lower latency under normal operation
fully ACID systems are PC/EC: they pay the availability and latency costs to keep consistency
PNUTS is PC/EL: normal operation trades consistency for latency, but under partition it gives up availability instead

sources.source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007)

items.item: Dynamo sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios to achieve a highly available, always-on experience
Dynamo provides eventual consistency, allowing updates to propagate to all replicas asynchronously

at.step: Predict: does a partition-time choice carry over to normal operation?

sources.source: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database (Corbett et al., OSDI 2012)

items.item: Spanner is a globally-distributed, synchronously-replicated database, the first to support externally-consistent distributed transactions at global scale

The CAP theorem is often misquoted as a permanent 'pick two' choice; Brewer's own retrospective is explicit that it only forbids perfect consistency and availability during the rare moments a partition actually exists — outside one, nothing stops a system from being fully consistent and available at once.

A system doesn't have to make one CAP choice for its whole lifetime, or even for a whole request — Brewer notes the choice can be made per-operation, at very fine granularity, which is why 'this system is CP' is often a simplification of what the system actually does under real partitions.

PACELC's real contribution isn't adding a fourth letter for its own sake — it's naming that a system's partition-time choice and its normal-case choice usually come from the same underlying design decision, which is why Dynamo's PA and EL aren't a coincidence.

Spanner's own TrueTime API is what lets it be PC/EC at global scale without unacceptable latency — bounded clock uncertainty lets it know when a transaction's timestamp is safely in the past, rather than needing a round trip to find out.

Classifying a system's PACELC quadrant from its own documentation, rather than from how it behaves in a specific deployment, is itself a methodological choice this topic makes deliberately — a misconfigured or unusually deployed system can behave outside its own documented quadrant, which this topic's own claims don't cover.

PNUTS is the system that breaks the intuition that PACELC's two halves always move together — its own PC/EL classification shows normal-case and partition-time choices can be decoupled on purpose, not just as a byproduct of a system nobody designed carefully.

A failure domain's containment is asymmetric by design: knowing a process crashed tells you nothing about its host, rack, zone or region, but knowing a region failed tells you everything inside it also failed — the two directions of inference are not mirror images of each other.

Google's own 'primary partition usually resides within one datacenter' design is itself a CAP-aware engineering choice, not an accident — by keeping consensus traffic inside domains where true partitions are rare, Google can afford to design as if CA holds most of the time.

'Effectively CA' is a statement about the observed probability of partitions in a specific, controlled network, not an exception to the theorem — the same system deployed across an uncontrolled wide-area network would face CAP's choice far more often.

This topic's own 'Prove it' answer generalizes beyond a single host crash: the same reasoning (only the contained domains are affected, the containing domains are untouched) applies identically whether the failure is a process, a rack, or an entire availability zone.
